beats.beat: The company operates in two segments: creation of infrastructure and operating a ready-mix concrete (RMC) plant.

On the infrastructure side, it executes railway contracts — platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion, laying railway tracks — bridge works across beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss forms, and bituminous and concrete road construction.

Work is won through tenders: a client floats a tender, a pre-bid meeting is held, the contractor bids, the job is awarded to the lowest quote, the contractor deposits a performance guarantee, and then drawings are issued and the site is handed over.

Its major clients are government bodies and their contractors: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation Ltd, MMRDA, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Ltd, plus private names such as Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.
That client list is also a dependency. Western Railway has been a client since 2006, contributes 52% of the orders on hand, and revenue from key customers was 57% of total revenue in fiscal 2018.

The company's own list of strengths includes cost efficiency, timely delivery, technical expertise and quality, the use of the box-pushing construction technique, and a leadership team with more than 20 years of infrastructure industry experience.

beats.beat: Revenue from operations fell from ₹90.21 crore in FY2015 to ₹60.53 crore in FY2018. The full path across the restated period: ₹86.61 crore in FY2014, ₹90.21 crore in FY2015, ₹74.53 crore in FY2016, ₹73.44 crore in FY2017, ₹60.53 crore in FY2018.

Net profit after adjustments was ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 — a sharp jump from ₹0.16 crore a year earlier, but still under the ₹0.96 crore reported for FY2014. The series: ₹0.96 crore, ₹0.78 crore, ₹0.33 crore, ₹0.16 crore, ₹3.15 crore.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax — the closest disclosed proxy to EBITDA — moved in line with revenue: ₹7.84 crore in FY2014, ₹9.46 crore in FY2015, ₹7.83 crore in FY2016, ₹6.76 crore in FY2017, ₹9.29 crore in FY2018.

The balance sheet is short-term-debt heavy. Short-term borrowings rose from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014 to ₹35.37 crore in FY2018, while long-term borrowings fell from ₹5.87 crore to ₹1.33 crore over the same period.
Total assets stood at ₹82.32 crore at FY2018 end, up from ₹70.62 crore four years earlier.
The filing itself flags that the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and warns that sustained negative cash flow could hurt its business and results.

beats.beat: The promoter is Amit Bholanath Mishra, who holds 74,95,476 equity shares — 90.949% of pre-issue paid-up equity share capital.

The other directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — each hold just 300 shares. The CFO is Anchal Pachori, a chartered accountant, and the company secretary and compliance officer is Mohit Soni.
One key management person, Hatim Sakerwala, holds 9% of the equity shares.
Related-party transactions in FY2018 included loans taken from KMP/board members of ₹68.4 lakh, director remuneration of ₹57.7 lakh, and outstanding payables to related parties of ₹324.3 lakh.

On litigation and conduct, the DRHP says litigation is pending at various stages; it also says no director is on the RBI willful-defaulter list and no criminal cases have been filed against the directors. But two companies promoted by the promoter — Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited — were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation.
The company also discloses that it has issued equity shares in the last 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price.

beats.beat: The DRHP describes the construction sector as highly fragmented and working-capital intensive, contributing roughly 8% to India's GDP at constant prices.

Demand is being supported by government flagship programmes — 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All — eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including real estate and construction, and rising urbanisation, industrialisation and disposable incomes.

The filing cites India's infrastructure investment requirement of ₹50 trillion by 2022, US$24.67 billion of FDI into construction development from April 2000 to December 2017, and a logistics sector expected to grow from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020 — a CAGR of 10.5%.
Competition is described only as spread across organised and unorganised players; the filing names no specific competitors.
The headwinds the company lists in its own SWOT are also the sector's: slow pace of government projects, working-capital crunches that may hit profitability, and changes in government policies.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-based infrastructure contractor and ready-mix concrete producer. It builds railway stations, bridges and roads for government bodies, and it sells concrete from a plant at Kashimira in Thane, Maharashtra.
The company is offering 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price that has not yet been fixed, with proceeds earmarked mainly for working capital. The listing is aimed at the SME Board.
The rest of this report walks through the business, the market, the five-year financial history disclosed in the DRHP, and the risks the filing itself flags.

beats.beat: The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at an issue price that is yet to be determined — the DRHP has not set a price.
The issue section names only the Equity Shares Offered; there is no offer-for-sale line and no selling shareholder in the excerpt, so the issue appears to be entirely fresh shares.
The lead manager to the issue is Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited and the registrar is Bigshare Services Private Limited.
The disclosed objects of the issue are: ₹1,130 lakh to meet working capital requirements, and general corporate purposes, for which the amount is not disclosed.

The filing also discloses that no independent agency has appraised the proposed project and no monitoring agency has been appointed; fund deployment will be at the discretion of management and the board, monitored by the audit committee.

beats.beat: Client concentration: Indian Railways is the largest customer, contributing 57% of revenue in fiscal 2018. Losing it would produce a significant drop in revenue and profitability.

Tender dependence: revenue depends on winning bids from government and PSU clients, which are awarded largely to the lowest quote; if bids are not accepted or if order-book contracts are cancelled or suspended, revenue and earnings will be hit.

Cash and debt stress: the company had negative cash flow in recent years, short-term borrowings stood at ₹35.37 crore at FY2018-end, and there was an unsecured loan of ₹405.02 lakh repayable on demand.
Geography concentration: a major portion of revenue comes from operations in Mumbai, and adverse developments in that region could have an outsized impact on revenue and results.

Governance and control concentration: the promoter holds 90.949% pre-issue, related-party transactions exist, no independent project appraisal or monitoring agency has been appointed, and two promoter-promoted companies were struck off by the ROC.

beats.beat: The basis-for-issue-price table shows three yearly per-share values — ₹1.31, ₹0.63 and ₹12.59 for FY2016, FY2017 and FY2018 — and a second set of per-share values — ₹4.14, ₹1.97 and ₹28.14 for the same years. The excerpt does not spell out the row labels, so the report will present them exactly as the filing does rather than guess at EPS, NAV or RoNW labels.

The DRHP says the issue price is to be determined by the company in consultation with the lead manager and is justified based on the accounting ratios, but the price itself and its multiple on the ₹10 face value are redacted.

A peer comparison table appears on page 55 with numeric values of 12.39 and 44.71 against the company's 28.14, and a revenue figure of ₹6,053.05 lakh, but the excerpt does not name the peers or label the multiples. A peer-based implied price range therefore cannot be computed from the material available.
The takeaway for a reader: valuation is unresolved in the DRHP — no price band, no named peer multiples, and no computed range.
